Five hundred poisoned examples can be consequential, but the count alone predicts neither success nor detectability: dataset size, duplication, model capacity, trigger coverage, and training choices matter. A backdoor can preserve ordinary validation accuracy while changing behavior on a narrow condition. Controlled sleeper-agent research illustrates why subsequent safety training is not proof that a backdoor was removed. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05566)

Defensively preserve data provenance, audit unexpected clusters and label changes, constrain dataset access, and compare clean and targeted evaluation slices in an isolated environment. Use trusted held-out data, model/version lineage, and rollback. Test for persistence after mitigation and monitor suspicious conditional behavior. Do not infer cleanliness from average benchmark scores; equally, an unusual input response is not sufficient evidence that deliberate poisoning occurred.
